blogs.title: The Pala Empire: Bengal’s Buddhist Golden Age
blogs.excerpt: How an elected king and his successors turned Bengal into the intellectual capital of Buddhist Asia.
blogs.author: History Bioscope Editorial
blogs.content:
## An elected king

Around 750 CE, after a century of anarchy known as **matsyanyaya** — "the law of the fish", where the big devour the small — the chiefs of Bengal did something extraordinary: they *chose* a king. His name was **Gopala**, and the dynasty he founded ruled for some four hundred years.

## Monasteries that drew the world

Gopala's son **Dharmapala** fought for supremacy over North India, but his lasting legacy was intellectual. He founded **Vikramashila** and the vast **Somapura Mahavihara** at Paharpur in today's Naogaon district. Pilgrims and scholars came from Tibet, China and Southeast Asia.

> Somapura's cruciform temple and 177 monastic cells made it one of the largest Buddhist monasteries south of the Himalayas.

## Art in terracotta

More than 2,000 terracotta plaques at Paharpur show daily life: farmers, musicians, animals and gods. Together with the bronze sculptures of the "Pala school", they influenced art from Nepal to Java.

## The scholar who went to Tibet

In the 11th century, **Atisha Dipankara** of Bikrampur left Vikramashila for Tibet, where his teachings reshaped Tibetan Buddhism. Bengal's influence on Asia had never been greater.

### Explore further
- Visit the *Somapura Mahavihara* event on the timeline
- Open the Map Explorer and toggle the **Pala Empire** territory layer

blogs.title: Muslin: The Fabric That Clothed the World
blogs.excerpt: Dhaka muslin was so fine it was called "woven air". Here is the story of its rise and fall.
blogs.author: History Bioscope Editorial
blogs.content:
## Woven air

Travellers called it *baft-hawa* — **woven air**. Dhaka muslin was spun from **Phuti karpas**, a cotton that grew only along the banks of the Meghna. Spinners worked in the humid early morning so the delicate thread would not snap.

## A global luxury

Under the Mughals, Bengal was one of the most productive regions on earth. Muslin dressed Mughal emperors and, by the 18th century, the fashionable women of Paris and London. Dutch, English, French and Armenian merchants competed for it.

## Decline

After Plassey (1757), the East India Company controlled weavers and prices. Then came the **Industrial Revolution**: machine-made Lancashire cotton flooded Indian markets while Indian cloth faced British tariffs. By the mid-19th century the great muslin tradition had vanished.

## Revival

In recent years Bangladeshi researchers have worked to identify the original Phuti karpas plant and recreate the fabric — a project to rescue a lost heritage.

blogs.title: 21 February: How a Language Made a Nation
blogs.excerpt: From a student protest in Dhaka to International Mother Language Day — the story of Ekushey.
blogs.author: History Bioscope Editorial
blogs.content:
## "Urdu and only Urdu"

In March 1948, Muhammad Ali Jinnah told a Dhaka audience that **Urdu** alone would be Pakistan's state language — although Bengali speakers were the majority of Pakistan's population. Students protested immediately.

## Ekushey February

On **21 February 1952**, students at Dhaka University defied a ban on gatherings. Police opened fire near the Medical College. **Salam, Barkat, Rafiq, Jabbar** and others were killed. A memorial built overnight was destroyed; it was later rebuilt as the **Shaheed Minar**.

## From language to nation

The movement turned language into the core of a new political identity. The same students and ideas fed the 1954 United Front victory, the 1966 Six Points, and ultimately the Liberation War of 1971.

## A gift to the world

In 1999 UNESCO declared 21 February **International Mother Language Day**. Every year, people around the world honour linguistic diversity because of the sacrifice made in Dhaka.

*"Amar bhaiyer rokte rangano Ekushey February, ami ki bhulite pari?"*

blogs.title: Inside Baghdad’s House of Wisdom
blogs.excerpt: Translators, mathematicians and astronomers turned Abbasid Baghdad into the world’s knowledge capital.
blogs.author: History Bioscope Editorial
blogs.content:
## A city of round walls and open minds

In 762 the caliph **al-Mansur** founded Baghdad as a round city on the Tigris. Within decades it became the largest city in the world, linking trade routes from China to Spain.

## The translation movement

Under **Harun al-Rashid** and especially **al-Ma'mun**, scholars translated Greek, Syriac, Persian and Sanskrit works into Arabic. **Hunayn ibn Ishaq** translated Galen and Hippocrates; others worked on Euclid, Ptolemy and Indian astronomy.

## Algebra and algorithms

**Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi** wrote *al-Kitab al-Mukhtasar fi Hisab al-Jabr wal-Muqabala*. "Al-jabr" gave us **algebra**, and the Latin form of his name, *Algoritmi*, gave us **algorithm**.

## Paper changes everything

Paper-making, learned from Chinese craftsmen in Samarkand, made books cheap. Baghdad's markets had whole streets of booksellers.

## Legacy

When the Mongols sacked Baghdad in 1258, it was said the Tigris ran black with ink. But the knowledge had already spread — to Cairo, Córdoba, and through Latin translations to the universities of Europe.

blogs.title: Walking the Silk Road
blogs.excerpt: Silk, paper, faith and plague — what really travelled along history’s greatest trade network.
blogs.author: History Bioscope Editorial
blogs.content:
## Not one road

The "Silk Road" — a term coined in the 19th century — was really a web of caravan routes across deserts and mountains, from **Chang'an** to **Samarkand**, **Baghdad** and **Constantinople**.

## What moved

- **Goods:** silk, porcelain, spices, horses, glass, paper
- **Ideas:** Buddhism to China, Islam to Central Asia, mathematics and astronomy in every direction
- **Technology:** paper-making, the compass, gunpowder
- **Disease:** the Black Death travelled along these routes in the 1340s

## The Mongol peace

Under the Mongols in the 13th–14th centuries, a merchant could, it was said, cross Asia safely. Marco Polo and Ibn Battuta both travelled in this world.

## Explore it on the map

Open the **Map Explorer**, enable the *Trade Routes* layer and press **Animate** to watch the Silk Road come alive.

blogs.title: From ARPANET to AI: Seventy Years of Computing
blogs.excerpt: How a few connected computers in 1969 led to the generative AI revolution.
blogs.author: History Bioscope Editorial
blogs.content:
## 1969: "LO"

The first ARPANET message between UCLA and SRI was supposed to be "LOGIN". The system crashed after two letters. History's first network message was **"LO"**.

## 1991: the Web

At CERN, **Tim Berners-Lee** combined hypertext with the Internet. The World Wide Web made the network usable by everyone.

## 2007: the Internet in your pocket

Smartphones and social media connected billions — including millions of Bangladeshis who skipped desktop computers entirely.

## 2017: attention

The paper *"Attention Is All You Need"* introduced the **Transformer**. It became the foundation of large language models.

## 2022 onwards: generative AI

AI assistants moved from labs to classrooms and offices within months. For students and researchers, the question is no longer *whether* to use AI, but *how* to use it responsibly.

events.title: Wari-Bateshwar Fortified Settlement
events.summary: One of the oldest urban sites in Bangladesh, with fortifications, roads and evidence of long-distance trade.
events.description: Excavations at Wari-Bateshwar on the old Brahmaputra have uncovered a fortified mud wall, a paved road, punch-marked silver coins, rouletted ware and semi-precious stone beads. Many scholars link it to "Sounagoura", a trading town named by the geographer Ptolemy.
events.significance: Shows that the Bengal delta was part of Indian Ocean trade networks reaching the Roman world more than 2,000 years ago.

events.title: Pundranagara (Mahasthangarh)
events.summary: The earliest known city of Bangladesh, capital of the ancient Pundravardhana region.
events.description: A limestone inscription in Brahmi script found at Mahasthangarh, dated to the Mauryan era, records a royal order on famine relief. The walled citadel on the Karatoya river was occupied continuously under the Mauryas, Guptas, Palas and Senas.
events.significance: Proves that northern Bengal was an organised administrative centre in the Mauryan period.

events.title: Shashanka, First Independent King of Gauda
events.summary: Shashanka built the first major independent kingdom in Bengal, ruling from Karnasuvarna.
events.description: Following the decline of the Gupta Empire, Shashanka united much of Bengal and expanded into Bihar and Odisha. He was a contemporary and rival of Harsha of Kannauj, and the Bengali calendar (Bangabda) is sometimes traced to his reign.
events.significance: The first time Bengal emerged as a distinct political power in North India.

events.title: Matsyanyaya – The Age of Anarchy
events.summary: A century of political chaos in Bengal after Shashanka, described as "the law of the fish".
events.description: With no central authority, local chiefs fought one another, much like big fish eating small fish. Texts and the Khalimpur copper plate describe how this disorder led the people to choose a ruler.
events.significance: The breakdown that set the stage for the election of Gopala and the rise of the Pala Empire.

events.title: Shalban Vihara and the Deva Dynasty at Mainamati
events.summary: A large Buddhist monastery in the Samatata kingdom of south-eastern Bengal.
events.description: The Shalban Vihara, attributed to Bhavadeva of the Deva dynasty, has 115 monks’ cells around a central shrine. Copper plates, terracotta plaques and coins from Mainamati show a thriving Buddhist culture in eastern Bengal.
events.significance: One of the best-preserved records of early-medieval Buddhist monastic life in the delta.

events.title: Gopala Founds the Pala Empire
events.summary: Gopala was chosen king by local chiefs, beginning four centuries of Pala rule.
events.description: The Palas were Buddhist rulers who patronised great monastic universities and art. At its height the empire stretched from Bengal across North India to Kannauj, and contested the Gangetic plain with the Gurjara-Pratiharas and Rashtrakutas.
events.significance: Bengal’s longest-ruling dynasty and the most important period of its ancient history.

events.title: Dharmapala and the Vikramashila University
events.summary: Dharmapala expanded the Pala Empire and founded the Vikramashila monastic university.
events.description: Dharmapala fought the Pratiharas and Rashtrakutas in the "tripartite struggle" for Kannauj. He founded Vikramashila and the Somapura Mahavihara, which together with Nalanda attracted scholars from Tibet, Southeast Asia and China.
events.significance: Made Bengal a centre of Buddhist learning for the whole of Asia.

events.title: Somapura Mahavihara (Paharpur) Built
events.summary: One of the largest Buddhist monasteries south of the Himalayas, now a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
events.description: Built under Dharmapala, the vihara has 177 cells arranged around a massive cruciform temple decorated with more than 2,000 terracotta plaques. Its architecture influenced temples as far away as Java and Myanmar.
events.significance: A UNESCO World Heritage Site (1985) and the finest monument of the Pala age.

events.title: Devapala’s Expansion
events.summary: Under Devapala the Pala Empire reached its greatest extent.
events.description: Inscriptions claim Devapala’s campaigns reached Assam, Odisha and the north-west. He maintained diplomatic ties with the Shailendra dynasty of Java, granting villages to support a monastery built at Nalanda by the Javanese king Balaputradeva.
events.significance: The peak of Bengal’s ancient imperial power and its maritime links with Southeast Asia.

events.title: Charyapada – Earliest Bengali Literature
events.summary: Mystical Buddhist songs that are the oldest surviving examples of the Bengali language.
events.description: The Charyapada are 47 songs composed by Sahajiya Buddhist poets (siddhacharyas). Haraprasad Shastri discovered the manuscript in the Nepal Royal Court Library in 1907.
events.significance: The foundation text of Bengali literature and language.

events.title: Chandra Dynasty of Vikrampur
events.summary: A Buddhist dynasty that ruled south-eastern Bengal from Vikrampur.
events.description: Copper plates of Srichandra and other kings show the Chandras controlled Harikela, Vanga and Samatata. Vikrampur became a leading political and cultural centre in eastern Bengal.
events.significance: Kept eastern Bengal politically distinct and established Vikrampur as a capital.

events.title: Atisha Dipankara Travels to Tibet
events.summary: The Bengali scholar Atisha revived Buddhism in Tibet.
events.description: Born in Bikrampur, Atisha Dipankara Srijnana became a senior teacher at Vikramashila. Invited by Tibetan rulers, he went to Tibet around 1042 and wrote influential works such as the "Lamp for the Path to Enlightenment".
events.significance: Bengal’s most influential scholar abroad; still revered across Tibetan Buddhism.

events.title: Rise of the Sena Dynasty
events.summary: The Hindu Sena dynasty replaced the Palas and ruled all of Bengal.
events.description: Originating from Karnataka, Samanta Sena’s descendants Vijaya Sena and Ballala Sena overthrew the declining Palas. They promoted Brahmanical Hinduism and introduced social reforms including the Kulinism system.
events.significance: Shifted Bengal from Buddhist to Brahmanical patronage before the Turkish conquest.

events.title: Lakshmana Sena and the Gita Govinda
events.summary: The last great Sena king, whose court produced classic Sanskrit poetry.
events.description: Lakshmana Sena’s court poets included Jayadeva, author of the Gita Govinda. After Bakhtiyar Khalji’s raid on Nadia, the king withdrew to eastern Bengal where his successors ruled for a few more decades.
events.significance: Marks the end of the ancient period and the high point of Sanskrit literature in Bengal.

events.title: Bakhtiyar Khalji Conquers Nadia
events.summary: A Turkic general captured the Sena capital, beginning Muslim rule in Bengal.
events.description: According to Minhaj-i-Siraj, Bakhtiyar Khalji reached Nadia with a small advance party of horsemen and surprised the palace. He established his capital at Lakhnauti (Gaur) under the nominal authority of the Delhi Sultanate.
events.significance: The start of more than five centuries of Muslim rule in Bengal.

events.title: Shah Jalal Arrives in Sylhet
events.summary: The Sufi saint Shah Jalal settled in Sylhet after its conquest from Raja Gour Govinda.
events.description: Shah Jalal and his companions accompanied the army of Sultan Shamsuddin Firuz Shah’s commander Sikandar Khan Ghazi and Nasiruddin. His shrine (dargah) in Sylhet remains one of the most visited sites in Bangladesh. Ibn Battuta visited him in 1345–46.
events.significance: Sufi missionaries played a central role in the spread of Islam in eastern Bengal.

events.title: Ibn Battuta Visits Bengal
events.summary: The Moroccan traveller described Bengal as "a hell full of good things".
events.description: Ibn Battuta landed at Chittagong, visited Shah Jalal in Sylhet, and travelled by river to Sonargaon before sailing to Java and China. He recorded how cheap rice, cloth and goods were in Bengal.
events.significance: One of the most vivid outside accounts of medieval Bengal’s prosperity.

events.title: Ilyas Shah Unites Bengal – Bengal Sultanate
events.summary: Shamsuddin Ilyas Shah unified Lakhnauti, Satgaon and Sonargaon into one independent sultanate.
events.description: Ilyas Shah took the title "Shah-i-Bangalah" and resisted invasions by Firuz Shah Tughlaq of Delhi. The Bengal Sultanate became a wealthy maritime power, trading textiles and rice across the Indian Ocean and exchanging embassies with Ming China.
events.significance: The first time "Bangalah" became the name of a unified, independent state.

events.title: Adina Mosque Built
events.summary: Sultan Sikandar Shah built what was then the largest mosque in the Indian subcontinent.
events.description: The Adina Mosque was a hypostyle mosque with hundreds of domes and a vast courtyard, built of brick and stone in the Bengali-Persian style. It proclaimed the Ilyas Shahi dynasty’s imperial ambition.
events.significance: A landmark of Bengal Sultanate architecture.

events.title: Ghiyasuddin Azam Shah, Hafez and Ming China
events.summary: A Bengal sultan famous for justice, poetry and diplomacy with China and Persia.
events.description: Ghiyasuddin Azam Shah corresponded with the Persian poet Hafez of Shiraz and sent embassies to the Ming court. Admiral Zheng He’s fleet visited Bengal in the early 15th century; a Bengal envoy famously presented a giraffe to the Yongle Emperor in 1414.
events.significance: Shows Bengal’s place in the cultural and diplomatic world of Asia.

events.title: Khan Jahan Ali and the Sixty Dome Mosque
events.summary: Khan Jahan Ali founded the mosque city of Khalifatabad in the Sundarbans.
events.description: Khan Jahan cleared forest land, built roads, ponds and mosques, and founded the city now known as Bagerhat. The Shat Gombuj (Sixty Dome) Mosque actually has 77 domes over its prayer hall.
events.significance: The Mosque City of Bagerhat is a UNESCO World Heritage Site (1985).

events.title: Alauddin Husain Shah – Golden Age of the Sultanate
events.summary: Husain Shah’s reign brought political stability and a flowering of Bengali literature.
events.description: He extended the sultanate to Kamrup and Arakan borders and patronised Bengali translations of the Mahabharata and Ramayana. The Bhakti saint Chaitanya Mahaprabhu was active in this period.
events.significance: Bengali emerged as a literary language under royal patronage.

events.title: Portuguese Arrive at Chittagong (Porto Grande)
events.summary: Portuguese traders and adventurers established a presence at "Porto Grande de Bengala".
events.description: From 1517 the Portuguese traded at Chittagong and Satgaon ("Porto Pequeno"). Some later allied with Arakan and engaged in piracy and slave raiding along the coast until the Mughal conquest of Chittagong in 1666.
events.significance: The first European colonial presence in Bengal.

events.title: Sher Shah Suri Takes Gaur
events.summary: The Afghan ruler Sher Shah conquered Bengal and later defeated the Mughal emperor Humayun.
events.description: Sher Shah captured Gaur in 1538 and defeated Humayun at Chausa (1539) and Kannauj (1540). He built or rebuilt the Grand Trunk Road from Sonargaon to the north-west and introduced the silver rupiya coin.
events.significance: His road and revenue system shaped South Asian administration for centuries.

events.title: Isa Khan and the Baro-Bhuiyans
events.summary: A confederacy of twelve landlords of the Bhati (lowland) region resisted Mughal conquest.
events.description: Led by Isa Khan of Sonargaon and later his son Musa Khan, the Baro-Bhuiyans used river fleets to fight Mughal armies. Isa Khan defeated a Mughal force at Egarasindur in 1597. Resistance ended when Islam Khan subdued Musa Khan in 1611.
events.significance: A symbol of Bengal’s regional independence against imperial power.

events.title: Battle of Rajmahal – Mughal Conquest
events.summary: Akbar’s army defeated Daud Khan Karrani, ending the independent Bengal Sultanate.
events.description: Mughal commanders Khan Jahan Husain Quli and Raja Todar Mal defeated and executed Daud Khan Karrani. Bengal became a Mughal province (subah), though local resistance continued for decades.
events.significance: Brought Bengal into the Mughal Empire.

events.title: Dhaka Becomes Capital (Jahangirnagar)
events.summary: Subahdar Islam Khan Chishti moved the provincial capital to Dhaka and named it Jahangirnagar.
events.description: Dhaka’s river location helped control the eastern delta and fight the Baro-Bhuiyans and Arakanese. The city grew into a major trading and textile centre.
events.significance: The beginning of Dhaka as the political centre of eastern Bengal.

events.title: Bara Katra and Shah Shuja’s Dhaka
events.summary: Prince Shah Shuja governed Bengal and built grand caravanserais in Dhaka.
events.description: Bara Katra (1644) was built under Shah Shuja as a residence and inn for travelling merchants on the Buriganga. Shah Shuja later lost the war of succession to Aurangzeb and fled to Arakan in 1660.
events.significance: Shows Dhaka’s status as a wealthy Mughal trading city.

events.title: Shaista Khan, Chittagong and Lalbagh Fort
events.summary: Shaista Khan conquered Chittagong from Arakan and presided over prosperous Dhaka.
events.description: In 1666 Mughal forces took Chittagong, ending Arakanese-Portuguese raids. Rice was famously so cheap that "eight maunds per rupee" was recorded. Prince Muhammad Azam began Lalbagh Fort in 1678.
events.significance: The height of Mughal Dhaka’s power and prosperity.

events.title: Dhaka Muslin and Bengal’s Textile Economy
events.summary: Bengal was one of the world’s leading producers of textiles, especially fine Dhaka muslin.
events.description: Spun from the Phuti karpas cotton grown along the Meghna, Dhaka muslin was prized in Mughal courts and European salons. Bengal exported cotton and silk cloth, saltpetre, rice and sugar through Dutch, English, French and Asian merchants.
events.significance: Mughal Bengal was among the most commercialised regions of the early modern world.

events.title: Murshid Quli Khan and the Nawabs of Bengal
events.summary: The diwan Murshid Quli Khan moved the capital to Murshidabad and founded the Nawabi regime.
events.description: As Mughal power weakened after Aurangzeb, Murshid Quli Khan became hereditary Nawab while still remitting revenue to Delhi. Bengal became effectively autonomous.
events.significance: The transition from Mughal province to semi-independent Nawabi state.

events.title: Alivardi Khan and the Maratha Raids
events.summary: Alivardi Khan defended Bengal from repeated Maratha (Bargi) invasions.
events.description: Between 1741 and 1751 Maratha cavalry raided western Bengal, causing great destruction remembered in folk lullabies. Alivardi eventually ceded Odisha revenues to make peace. His grandson Siraj ud-Daulah succeeded him in 1756.
events.significance: Weakened Bengal’s economy on the eve of British conquest.

events.title: East India Company Founds Calcutta
events.summary: Job Charnock of the English East India Company established a trading post at Sutanuti.
events.description: In 1698 the Company bought the zamindari of Sutanuti, Gobindapur and Kalikata. Fort William was built to protect its trade, and Calcutta grew into the base of British power in India.
events.significance: The foundation of what became the capital of British India until 1911.

events.title: Battle of Plassey
events.summary: Robert Clive’s East India Company forces defeated Nawab Siraj ud-Daulah.
events.description: The battle was decided largely by the betrayal of the Nawab’s commander Mir Jafar, who held back his troops. Siraj was captured and killed, and Mir Jafar was installed as a puppet Nawab.
events.significance: Began nearly 190 years of British rule in Bengal and the subcontinent.

events.title: Battle of Buxar and the Diwani
events.summary: The Company defeated an alliance of Mir Qasim, the Nawab of Awadh and the Mughal emperor.
events.description: By the Treaty of Allahabad (1765), Emperor Shah Alam II granted the Company the Diwani, the right to collect revenue in Bengal, Bihar and Odisha.
events.significance: Turned a trading company into the ruler of Bengal.

events.title: Great Bengal Famine
events.summary: A catastrophic famine killed an estimated one-third of Bengal’s population.
events.description: Drought, crop failure and the Company’s rigid revenue collection combined to produce mass starvation. Estimates of deaths run into the millions.
events.significance: Exposed the human cost of Company rule and led to administrative reforms.

events.title: The Permanent Settlement
events.summary: Lord Cornwallis fixed land revenue permanently with zamindars.
events.description: The Permanent Settlement created a landed aristocracy of zamindars, many of them absentee landlords, while peasants bore heavy rents. It shaped rural social relations in Bengal well into the 20th century.
events.significance: Created the zamindari system that land reforms after 1950 sought to abolish.

events.title: Faraizi Movement and Titumir’s Revolt
events.summary: Religious reform movements turned into peasant resistance against landlords and indigo planters.
events.description: Haji Shariatullah founded the Faraizi movement in eastern Bengal; his son Dudu Miyan organised peasants against oppressive zamindars. Titumir built a bamboo fort at Narkelberia, destroyed by British troops in 1831.
events.significance: Early mass resistance to colonial and landlord oppression.

events.title: The Bengal Renaissance
events.summary: A cultural and intellectual awakening in literature, science, religion and social reform.
events.description: Figures such as Raja Rammohan Roy, Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar, Michael Madhusudan Dutt, Jagadish Chandra Bose and Rabindranath Tagore reshaped Bengali thought. Tagore wrote much of his work at Shilaidaha, and won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1913.
events.significance: Laid the cultural foundations of modern Bengali identity.

events.title: Revolt of 1857 and Crown Rule
events.summary: The great uprising against Company rule began among sepoys in Bengal.
events.description: Mangal Pandey’s attack at Barrackpore in March 1857 preceded the wider revolt at Meerut. In Dhaka, sepoys at Lalbagh were attacked and rebels were later hanged at what is now Bahadur Shah Park. In 1858 the British Crown took direct control of India.
events.significance: Ended the East India Company’s rule and the Mughal dynasty.

events.title: Partition of Bengal (1905)
events.summary: Lord Curzon split Bengal, creating the province of Eastern Bengal and Assam with Dhaka as capital.
events.description: The partition was opposed by the Swadeshi movement, mostly led by Bengali Hindus in Calcutta, and supported by many Muslims of the east. It was annulled in 1911 and the capital of India moved to Delhi.
events.significance: Sharpened Hindu–Muslim political divisions and briefly made Dhaka a provincial capital.

events.title: All-India Muslim League Founded in Dhaka
events.summary: The Muslim League was founded at a conference hosted by Nawab Salimullah in Dhaka.
events.description: Formed at the All India Muhammadan Educational Conference, the League aimed to protect Muslim political interests. Under Muhammad Ali Jinnah it later led the demand for Pakistan.
events.significance: The party that led the Pakistan movement was born in Dhaka.

events.title: University of Dhaka Founded
events.summary: The university was established partly as compensation for the annulment of the 1905 partition.
events.description: Dhaka University became the intellectual centre of East Bengal. Its students and teachers played leading roles in the Language Movement, the 1969 uprising and the Liberation War.
events.significance: The cradle of Bangladeshi nationalism.

events.title: Kazi Nazrul Islam’s "Bidrohi"
events.summary: The "Rebel Poet" published his poem Bidrohi, electrifying anti-colonial Bengal.
events.description: Nazrul’s poetry and songs combined Hindu and Muslim imagery and fierce protest against injustice. He was imprisoned by the British for his writings. Bangladesh later recognised him as its national poet.
events.significance: National Poet of Bangladesh; his songs inspired the Liberation War.

events.title: Lahore Resolution
events.summary: A.K. Fazlul Huq of Bengal moved the resolution demanding independent states for Muslims.
events.description: The text called for "independent States" in Muslim-majority regions of the north-west and east. Many Bengali politicians later argued this implied a separate eastern state, an argument revived during the struggle for autonomy.
events.significance: The founding document of the Pakistan movement.

events.title: Bengal Famine of 1943
events.summary: Between two and three million people died during a wartime famine.
events.description: Loss of rice imports from Burma, a cyclone, wartime inflation, hoarding and colonial policy priorities all contributed. Amartya Sen later used it to show that famines can occur without a collapse in food supply.
events.significance: A defining trauma of late colonial Bengal.

events.title: Partition: East Bengal Joins Pakistan
events.summary: British India was divided; Muslim-majority East Bengal became the eastern wing of Pakistan.
events.description: The Radcliffe Line split Bengal. East Bengal (renamed East Pakistan in 1955) was separated from West Pakistan by about 1,600 km of Indian territory. Millions crossed the new borders amid violence.
events.significance: Created the state structure from which Bangladesh would later emerge.

events.title: Language Movement – 21 February
events.summary: Students died defending Bangla as a state language of Pakistan.
events.description: After Jinnah declared in 1948 that Urdu alone would be the state language, protests grew. On 21 February 1952 police fired on students at Dhaka University and Medical College; Salam, Barkat, Rafiq, Jabbar and others were killed. Bengali was recognised as a state language in 1956.
events.significance: The birth of Bengali nationalism; 21 February is now International Mother Language Day.

events.title: United Front Victory
events.summary: The Jukto Front coalition crushed the Muslim League in the East Bengal elections.
events.description: Led by A.K. Fazlul Huq, H.S. Suhrawardy and Maulana Bhashani, the coalition ran on a 21-point programme including autonomy and recognition of Bengali. The central government dismissed the provincial ministry within weeks.
events.significance: Showed the Muslim League had lost East Bengal and foreshadowed the autonomy struggle.

events.title: Ayub Khan’s Martial Law
events.summary: General Ayub Khan seized power, centralising authority in West Pakistan.
events.description: Economic disparity between East and West Pakistan widened under Ayub’s "Decade of Development", as revenues from East Pakistan’s jute exports funded western development.
events.significance: Fuelled grievances that drove the Six Point Movement.

events.title: Six Point Movement
events.summary: Sheikh Mujibur Rahman presented six demands for East Pakistan’s autonomy.
events.description: Announced in Lahore in February 1966, the points demanded a federal system, separate currencies or controls on capital flight, provincial taxation, separate foreign-exchange accounts and a paramilitary force for the east. A general strike on 7 June 1966 saw protesters killed.
events.significance: Described as the "Magna Carta" of Bengali liberation.

events.title: Agartala Case and the 1969 Mass Uprising
events.summary: A mass uprising forced the release of Sheikh Mujib and the fall of Ayub Khan.
events.description: The government charged Sheikh Mujib and others with conspiring with India (the Agartala Conspiracy Case). Student-led protests, with the 11-point programme, brought millions onto the streets; Asaduzzaman (Asad) and Sergeant Zahurul Haq were among those killed. Mujib was freed and given the title "Bangabandhu".
events.significance: Made Sheikh Mujibur Rahman the undisputed leader of East Pakistan.

events.title: Bhola Cyclone
events.summary: One of the deadliest tropical cyclones ever recorded struck the coast of East Pakistan.
events.description: A storm surge swept over the islands and coastal districts, killing an estimated 300,000–500,000 people. The central government’s slow relief response deepened anger in the east.
events.significance: A humanitarian catastrophe that influenced the December 1970 election.

events.title: 1970 General Election
events.summary: The Awami League won an absolute majority in Pakistan’s National Assembly.
events.description: The Awami League won 160 of the 162 general seats from East Pakistan. President Yahya Khan and Zulfikar Ali Bhutto’s PPP refused to transfer power, and the assembly session was postponed on 1 March 1971.
events.significance: The refusal to honour the result led directly to the Liberation War.

events.title: Historic 7th March Speech
events.summary: "The struggle this time is the struggle for our freedom, the struggle this time is the struggle for independence."
events.description: Before a huge crowd, Sheikh Mujibur Rahman announced a non-cooperation movement and urged Bengalis to prepare for resistance. UNESCO added the speech to its Memory of the World Register in 2017.
events.significance: A defining call for independence.

events.title: Operation Searchlight
events.summary: The Pakistan Army launched a military crackdown on Bengali civilians, students and police.
events.description: On the night of 25 March, troops attacked Dhaka University halls, Rajarbagh Police Lines, the EPR headquarters and Hindu neighbourhoods. Sheikh Mujib was arrested and flown to West Pakistan. 25 March is observed as Genocide Day in Bangladesh.
events.significance: The start of the 1971 genocide and the armed Liberation War.

events.title: Declaration of Independence
events.summary: Bangladesh’s independence was declared; 26 March is Independence Day.
events.description: A message from Sheikh Mujibur Rahman declaring independence was circulated in the early hours of 26 March. It was broadcast from the Swadhin Bangla Betar Kendra at Kalurghat, Chattogram, including a declaration read by Major Ziaur Rahman on Mujib’s behalf on 27 March.
events.significance: The formal start of the independent state of Bangladesh.

events.title: Mujibnagar Government Formed
events.summary: The Provisional Government of Bangladesh took oath at Baidyanathtala, renamed Mujibnagar.
events.description: With Sheikh Mujib as President (in absentia), Syed Nazrul Islam as acting President and Tajuddin Ahmad as Prime Minister, the government led the war from exile in Calcutta and coordinated diplomacy and the armed forces under General M.A.G. Osmani.
events.significance: Gave the liberation struggle a legal and political leadership.

events.title: Mukti Bahini and the 11 Sectors
events.summary: Bengali soldiers, students, farmers and workers fought a nine-month guerrilla war.
events.description: The country was divided into 11 military sectors. Freedom fighters (Muktijoddha) disrupted Pakistani forces, while about 10 million refugees fled to India. Women suffered mass sexual violence, and hundreds of thousands to three million people were killed (estimates vary widely).
events.significance: The armed struggle at the heart of national independence.

events.title: Killing of Intellectuals
events.summary: Teachers, doctors, writers and journalists were abducted and killed days before victory.
events.description: The Pakistan Army and its collaborators (including the Al-Badr militia) targeted the Bengali intelligentsia to cripple the new nation. Bodies were found at Rayerbazar and Mirpur. 14 December is Martyred Intellectuals Day.
events.significance: A deliberate attempt to destroy the nation’s intellectual leadership.

events.title: Victory Day – Surrender in Dhaka
events.summary: Pakistani forces surrendered to the joint command of India and Bangladesh.
events.description: After India entered the war on 3 December, allied forces converged on Dhaka. Lt. Gen. A.A.K. Niazi signed the Instrument of Surrender before Lt. Gen. Jagjit Singh Aurora, with Group Captain A.K. Khandker representing Bangladesh. Around 93,000 Pakistani personnel became prisoners of war.
events.significance: The birth of independent Bangladesh.

events.title: Bangabandhu Returns Home
events.summary: Sheikh Mujibur Rahman returned from Pakistani prison via London and Delhi.
events.description: Released after the war, Mujib received a massive welcome in Dhaka and became Prime Minister. His government began rebuilding a war-ravaged country.
events.significance: Start of the reconstruction of Bangladesh.

events.title: Constitution of Bangladesh
events.summary: The Constituent Assembly adopted the constitution, effective 16 December 1972.
events.description: Drafted by a committee chaired by Dr. Kamal Hossain, it established a parliamentary democracy with nationalism, socialism, democracy and secularism as state principles.
events.significance: The founding legal framework of the republic.

events.title: Bangladesh Joins the United Nations
events.summary: Bangladesh became the 136th member of the UN; Mujib addressed the General Assembly in Bangla.
events.description: Pakistan recognised Bangladesh in February 1974, clearing the way for UN membership after a Chinese veto in 1972. Sheikh Mujib’s speech on 25 September 1974 was the first in Bengali at the UN.
events.significance: International acceptance of the new nation.

references.title: Wikipedia – Bangladesh and the United Nations

events.title: Assassination of Sheikh Mujibur Rahman
events.summary: Sheikh Mujib and most of his family were killed in a military coup.
events.description: A group of army officers attacked his residence at Dhanmondi Road 32. A series of coups followed, and on 3 November four national leaders were killed in Dhaka Central Jail. 15 August is observed as National Mourning Day.
events.significance: Began a long period of military and quasi-military rule.

references.title: Wikipedia – Assassination of Sheikh Mujibur Rahman

events.title: Presidency of Ziaur Rahman
events.summary: Ziaur Rahman became President and founded the Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP).
events.description: Zia introduced multi-party politics, promoted "Bangladeshi nationalism", expanded garment exports and proposed the SAARC regional forum. He was assassinated in Chattogram in May 1981.
events.significance: Shaped one of the country’s two main political traditions.

events.title: Ershad Era and the 1990 Uprising
events.summary: General H.M. Ershad ruled for nine years until a mass movement forced his resignation.
events.description: Ershad seized power in March 1982. Opposition parties and students united in a prolonged movement; the death of Dr. Milon and Nur Hossain became rallying symbols. Ershad resigned on 6 December 1990.
events.significance: Restored democratic government.

events.title: Return to Parliamentary Democracy
events.summary: A free election under a caretaker government made Khaleda Zia the first female Prime Minister.
events.description: The 12th amendment restored the parliamentary system. For the next three decades politics was dominated by rivalry between the BNP (Khaleda Zia) and the Awami League (Sheikh Hasina).
events.significance: The beginning of the modern democratic era.

events.title: Ganges Water Sharing Treaty and Chittagong Hill Tracts Accord
events.summary: Agreements on Ganges water with India and peace in the Chittagong Hill Tracts.
events.description: The 30-year Ganges treaty was signed in December 1996. The Chittagong Hill Tracts Peace Accord of December 1997 ended two decades of insurgency by the Shanti Bahini.
events.significance: Addressed two long-running regional conflicts.

references.title: Wikipedia – Chittagong Hill Tracts Peace Accord

events.title: International Mother Language Day
events.summary: UNESCO proclaimed 21 February as International Mother Language Day.
events.description: The proposal originated from Bangladeshi expatriates in Canada and was presented by Bangladesh. It has been observed worldwide since 2000 to promote linguistic and cultural diversity.
events.significance: Turned the sacrifice of 1952 into a global commemoration.

events.title: Nobel Peace Prize for Yunus and Grameen Bank
events.summary: Muhammad Yunus and Grameen Bank won the Nobel Peace Prize for microcredit.
events.description: Starting with small loans in Jobra village near Chittagong University in 1976, Grameen pioneered collateral-free lending, mostly to rural women. The model spread to many countries.
events.significance: Bangladesh’s first Nobel Prize.

events.title: Garment Industry Growth and Rana Plaza
events.summary: Bangladesh became the world’s second-largest garment exporter; the Rana Plaza collapse exposed safety failures.
events.description: Ready-made garments grew from a handful of factories in the late 1970s to the backbone of exports, employing millions of mostly women workers. On 24 April 2013 the Rana Plaza building collapsed in Savar, killing 1,134 people and leading to international safety accords.
events.significance: Defines both the success and the costs of Bangladesh’s export-led growth.

events.title: Rohingya Refugee Influx
events.summary: More than 700,000 Rohingya fled military violence in Myanmar to Bangladesh.
events.description: The camps near Cox’s Bazar became among the largest refugee settlements in the world, hosting around one million people. Bangladesh pursued repatriation talks and international support.
events.significance: One of the largest humanitarian crises of the 21st century.

events.title: Padma Multipurpose Bridge Opens
events.summary: The 6.15 km road-rail bridge connected the south-west of Bangladesh to the capital.
events.description: Built largely with domestic funding after the World Bank withdrew, the bridge cut travel times between Dhaka and 21 southern districts.
events.significance: A landmark infrastructure project for national connectivity.

events.title: July Uprising of 2024
events.summary: A student-led protest over job quotas became a mass uprising that ended Sheikh Hasina’s government.
events.description: Protests began over civil service quotas in July 2024. Abu Sayeed’s death in Rangpur and a violent crackdown killed hundreds and escalated the movement. Sheikh Hasina resigned and left the country on 5 August 2024; an interim government led by Muhammad Yunus took office on 8 August.
events.significance: A major political turning point in contemporary Bangladesh.

events.title: Adam (AS) – The First Human and Prophet
events.summary: Allah created Adam, taught him the names of all things, and made him a khalifah on earth.
events.description: The Quran describes Adam’s creation, the angels’ prostration, Iblis’s refusal, life in the Garden with Hawwa (Eve), the eating from the forbidden tree, and their repentance. Tradition associates their reunion on earth with Arafat.
events.significance: The father of humanity and the first prophet; his story teaches repentance and human responsibility. By Islamic tradition; dates are not historically fixed and the timeline position is illustrative.

events.title: Idris (AS)
events.summary: A truthful prophet whom Allah "raised to a high station" (Maryam 19:56–57).
events.description: Commonly identified with the biblical Enoch. Traditions credit him with being among the first to write with a pen and to study the stars and sewing.
events.significance: Example of truthfulness, knowledge and patience. By Islamic tradition; dates are not historically fixed and the timeline position is illustrative.

events.title: Nuh (AS) and the Great Flood
events.summary: Nuh preached for 950 years; the ark came to rest on al-Judi.
events.description: The Quran (Surah Nuh, Hud 11:25–49) describes his patient call to his people, their rejection, the building of the ark and the flood that saved the believers. The ark settled on Mount Judi.
events.significance: One of the five "Ulul-Azm" (resolute) messengers. By Islamic tradition; dates are not historically fixed and the timeline position is illustrative.

events.title: Hud (AS) and the People of ‘Ad
events.summary: Hud warned the powerful tribe of ‘Ad, who built lofty structures in the sand dunes of al-Ahqaf.
events.description: When ‘Ad rejected his message, a furious wind destroyed them over seven nights and eight days (Al-Haqqah 69:6–7). Iram "of the pillars" is linked with this people.
events.significance: Warns against arrogance in power and wealth. By Islamic tradition; dates are not historically fixed and the timeline position is illustrative.

events.title: Salih (AS) and the She-Camel of Thamud
events.summary: Salih was sent to Thamud, who carved homes from mountains; they killed the miraculous she-camel.
events.description: Allah sent a she-camel as a sign. Thamud hamstrung her and were destroyed by a mighty blast. The rock-cut site of al-Hijr, which the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ passed during the Tabuk expedition, is associated with them.
events.significance: A lesson in heeding divine signs. By Islamic tradition; dates are not historically fixed and the timeline position is illustrative.

events.title: Ibrahim (AS) – Khalilullah
events.summary: Ibrahim rejected idols, survived the fire, and with Ismail raised the foundations of the Ka‘bah.
events.description: He argued against the idol-worship of his people and the king (Nimrod), was thrown into a fire that Allah made "cool and safe", migrated to Canaan, and left Hajar and Ismail in the valley of Makkah. The rites of Hajj and Eid al-Adha commemorate his family’s sacrifice.
events.significance: Father of the prophets and a model of pure monotheism (hanif). By Islamic tradition; dates are not historically fixed and the timeline position is illustrative.

events.title: Lut (AS) and the Cities of the Plain
events.summary: Lut, nephew of Ibrahim, warned the people of Sodom against their immorality.
events.description: When they rejected him, angels instructed Lut to leave by night with his family (except his wife), and the towns were overturned and rained with stones of baked clay.
events.significance: A warning about moral corruption and its consequences. By Islamic tradition; dates are not historically fixed and the timeline position is illustrative.

events.title: Ismail (AS) and Zamzam
events.summary: Hajar’s search between Safa and Marwah ended with the spring of Zamzam for baby Ismail.
events.description: Ismail grew up in Makkah among the Jurhum tribe, submitted to the command of sacrifice, and helped Ibrahim build the Ka‘bah. He is the ancestor of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ through the Arabs of the Hejaz.
events.significance: The Sa‘i ritual of Hajj and the sanctity of Zamzam come from his story. By Islamic tradition; dates are not historically fixed and the timeline position is illustrative.

events.title: Ishaq (AS)
events.summary: Son of Ibrahim and Sarah, given as glad tidings in their old age.
events.description: Angels brought news of Ishaq’s birth to Ibrahim and Sarah. From him came the prophets of the Children of Israel through his son Yaqub.
events.significance: Ancestor of the Israelite prophets. By Islamic tradition; dates are not historically fixed and the timeline position is illustrative.

events.title: Yaqub (AS) – Israel
events.summary: Yaqub, also called Israel, was father of the twelve tribes.
events.description: The Quran highlights his "beautiful patience" (sabrun jamil) at the loss of Yusuf and his deathbed charge to his sons to worship the One God.
events.significance: Patriarch of the Children of Israel. By Islamic tradition; dates are not historically fixed and the timeline position is illustrative.

events.title: Yusuf (AS) in Egypt
events.summary: Surah Yusuf calls his story "the best of stories".
events.description: Thrown into a well by his brothers, sold into Egypt, wrongly imprisoned, and then raised to manage Egypt’s granaries after interpreting the king’s dream, Yusuf forgave his brothers and reunited his family.
events.significance: A story of patience, chastity and forgiveness. By Islamic tradition; dates are not historically fixed and the timeline position is illustrative.

events.title: Ayyub (AS) – The Patient
events.summary: Ayyub endured illness and loss with complete patience.
events.description: He called on his Lord: "Indeed, adversity has touched me, and You are the Most Merciful of the merciful" (Al-Anbiya 21:83). Allah restored his health, family and wealth.
events.significance: The model of patience (sabr) in suffering. By Islamic tradition; dates are not historically fixed and the timeline position is illustrative.

events.title: Shu‘ayb (AS) and Madyan
events.summary: Shu‘ayb called the people of Madyan to honest weights and measures.
events.description: His people cheated in trade and blocked the way of God. They were destroyed by an earthquake. Many traditions link him with the father-in-law of Musa in Madyan.
events.significance: A prophetic call for economic justice. By Islamic tradition; dates are not historically fixed and the timeline position is illustrative.

events.title: Musa (AS) – Exodus and the Torah
events.summary: The most frequently named prophet in the Quran, sent to Pharaoh with nine signs.
events.description: Rescued from the Nile as a baby, raised in Pharaoh’s palace, Musa fled to Madyan, received revelation at the burning bush, confronted Pharaoh, led the Israelites through the parted sea, and received the Torah at Sinai.
events.significance: One of the Ulul-Azm messengers; Kalimullah, "the one who spoke with Allah". By Islamic tradition; dates are not historically fixed and the timeline position is illustrative.

events.title: Harun (AS)
events.summary: Musa’s brother and eloquent helper.
events.description: Musa asked Allah to make Harun his minister. Harun led the Israelites while Musa was on the mountain and tried to stop them from worshipping the golden calf.
events.significance: An example of brotherly support in the mission. By Islamic tradition; dates are not historically fixed and the timeline position is illustrative.

events.title: Dhul-Kifl (AS)
events.summary: Mentioned among the patient and righteous (Al-Anbiya 21:85, Sad 38:48).
events.description: His identity is debated: some link him with the biblical Ezekiel, whose traditional shrine is at al-Kifl in Iraq. The Quran praises him without giving details of his story.
events.significance: Honoured for patience and fulfilling his pledges. By Islamic tradition; dates are not historically fixed and the timeline position is illustrative.

events.title: Dawud (AS) – King and Prophet
events.summary: Dawud defeated Jalut (Goliath) and received the Zabur (Psalms).
events.description: Allah gave Dawud kingship, wisdom and decisive judgment. Mountains and birds glorified Allah with him, and iron was made soft for him to make coats of mail.
events.significance: Combined prophethood with just rule. By Islamic tradition; dates are not historically fixed and the timeline position is illustrative.

events.title: Sulayman (AS) and the Queen of Sheba
events.summary: Sulayman was given command over the wind, the jinn and understanding of the speech of birds and ants.
events.description: The hoopoe brought news of the Queen of Saba’ (Bilqis), who came to Sulayman and submitted to Allah. He built a great sanctuary in Jerusalem.
events.significance: A prophet-king whose power was used in gratitude. By Islamic tradition; dates are not historically fixed and the timeline position is illustrative.

events.title: Ilyas (AS) and the Worship of Ba‘l
events.summary: Ilyas called his people away from the idol Ba‘l.
events.description: "Do you call upon Ba‘l and forsake the best of creators?" (As-Saffat 37:125). Identified with the biblical Elijah.
events.significance: Resistance to idolatry in the Israelite kingdoms. By Islamic tradition; dates are not historically fixed and the timeline position is illustrative.

events.title: Al-Yasa‘ (AS)
events.summary: Named among the chosen and the best (Sad 38:48).
events.description: Identified with the biblical Elisha, successor of Ilyas. The Quran mentions him alongside Ismail and Dhul-Kifl.
events.significance: Continuity of prophetic guidance. By Islamic tradition; dates are not historically fixed and the timeline position is illustrative.

events.title: Yunus (AS) and Nineveh
events.summary: Swallowed by a great fish, Yunus prayed: "There is no god but You; glory be to You; I was among the wrongdoers."
events.description: After leaving his people in anger, Yunus was cast into the sea. His supplication from the belly of the fish was answered, and his people of Nineveh believed—the only nation in the Quran saved after a warning.
events.significance: His prayer is recited by Muslims in distress. By Islamic tradition; dates are not historically fixed and the timeline position is illustrative.

events.title: Zakariya (AS)
events.summary: Guardian of Maryam, who prayed in old age for a righteous son.
events.description: Zakariya found provision miraculously with Maryam in her prayer niche (mihrab) and prayed for an heir; he was given glad tidings of Yahya.
events.significance: A model of hopeful supplication. By Islamic tradition; dates are not historically fixed and the timeline position is illustrative.

events.title: Yahya (AS)
events.summary: Son of Zakariya, given wisdom as a child, a confirmer of the word from Allah.
events.description: The Quran describes Yahya as dutiful, pure and chaste. He is identified with John the Baptist.
events.significance: Herald of Isa. By Islamic tradition; dates are not historically fixed and the timeline position is illustrative.

references.title: Wikipedia – John the Baptist in Islam

events.title: Isa (AS) – The Messiah, son of Maryam
events.summary: Born miraculously to the virgin Maryam, Isa received the Injil.
events.description: He spoke from the cradle, healed the blind and lepers and raised the dead by Allah’s permission. The Quran states he was not killed or crucified but raised by Allah, and Muslims believe he will return.
events.significance: One of the Ulul-Azm messengers; Surah Maryam honours his mother. By Islamic tradition; dates are not historically fixed and the timeline position is illustrative.

events.title: Birth of Muhammad ﷺ – Year of the Elephant
events.summary: The final Prophet was born in Makkah into the clan of Banu Hashim of Quraysh.
events.description: His father Abdullah died before his birth; he was nursed by Halimah among Banu Sa‘d, and raised by his grandfather Abd al-Muttalib and uncle Abu Talib. The year is remembered for Abraha’s failed elephant expedition against the Ka‘bah (Surah Al-Fil).
events.significance: The beginning of the life of the Seal of the Prophets.

events.title: Marriage to Khadijah (RA)
events.summary: Known as al-Amin (the trustworthy), Muhammad ﷺ married the merchant Khadijah.
events.description: He had managed Khadijah’s trade caravan to Syria with great honesty. She became the first person to believe in his prophethood and his greatest supporter.
events.significance: A partnership that sustained the early mission.

events.title: First Revelation in the Cave of Hira
events.summary: Angel Jibril brought the first verses: "Read in the name of your Lord who created" (Al-‘Alaq 96:1–5).
events.description: While in retreat in Hira, Muhammad ﷺ received revelation. Khadijah comforted him and took him to her cousin Waraqah ibn Nawfal. Revelation continued for about 23 years, forming the Quran.
events.significance: The beginning of the Quran and of Muhammad’s prophethood.

events.title: Migration to Abyssinia
events.summary: Persecuted Muslims found refuge with the just Christian king, the Negus (an-Najashi).
events.description: Ja‘far ibn Abi Talib recited Surah Maryam before the Negus, who refused Quraysh’s demand to hand the Muslims over.
events.significance: The first hijrah, and an early example of Muslim–Christian goodwill.

events.title: Year of Sorrow and the Isra & Mi‘raj
events.summary: After losing Khadijah and Abu Talib, the Prophet ﷺ was taken by night to Jerusalem and the heavens.
events.description: Rejected at Ta’if, the Prophet ﷺ was honoured with the Night Journey to al-Masjid al-Aqsa, where he led the prophets in prayer, and the Ascension, during which the five daily prayers were prescribed.
events.significance: Established the five daily prayers and the sanctity of al-Aqsa for Muslims.

events.title: The Hijrah to Madinah – 1 AH
events.summary: The Prophet ﷺ and Abu Bakr migrated to Yathrib, which became Madinat an-Nabi.
events.description: After the pledges of ‘Aqabah, Muslims migrated to Yathrib. The Prophet ﷺ and Abu Bakr hid in the Cave of Thawr, then travelled the coastal route. He built Masjid Quba and Masjid an-Nabawi, and the Constitution of Madinah united its communities.
events.significance: Year 1 of the Islamic (Hijri) calendar and the founding of the first Muslim polity.

events.title: Battle of Badr
events.summary: About 313 Muslims defeated a Quraysh army of around 1,000.
events.description: The Quran calls it Yawm al-Furqan, "the Day of Criterion". Abu Jahl and other Quraysh leaders were killed.
events.significance: Established the Muslim community of Madinah as a power in Arabia.

events.title: Battle of Uhud
events.summary: Quraysh avenged Badr after archers left their positions.
events.description: The Muslim army was initially winning, but the archers on the hill (Jabal ar-Rumah) left their posts. Khalid ibn al-Walid’s cavalry attacked from behind. Hamzah ibn Abd al-Muttalib was martyred.
events.significance: A lesson in obedience and discipline.

events.title: Battle of the Trench (Khandaq)
events.summary: Muslims dug a trench around Madinah to repel a 10,000-strong confederacy.
events.description: On Salman al-Farisi’s advice the Muslims dug a defensive trench. After a long siege, cold winds and disunity broke up the confederate alliance (Al-Ahzab).
events.significance: The last major Quraysh offensive against Madinah.

events.title: Treaty of Hudaybiyyah
events.summary: A ten-year truce with Quraysh that the Quran calls "a clear victory".
events.description: Though its terms seemed unfavourable, the peace allowed Islam to spread rapidly. The Prophet ﷺ sent letters to rulers including Heraclius, Khosrow II and the Negus.
events.significance: Diplomacy that opened Arabia to Islam.

events.title: Conquest of Makkah
events.summary: The Prophet ﷺ entered Makkah almost without bloodshed and declared a general amnesty.
events.description: After Quraysh allies broke the treaty, a 10,000-strong army entered Makkah. The 360 idols around the Ka‘bah were destroyed and the Prophet ﷺ forgave his former enemies.
events.significance: Restored the Ka‘bah to monotheism and united Arabia.

events.title: Farewell Pilgrimage and Passing of the Prophet ﷺ
events.summary: The Farewell Sermon at Arafat proclaimed human equality and sanctity of life and property.
events.description: "This day I have perfected for you your religion" (Al-Ma’idah 5:3) was revealed. The Prophet ﷺ passed away in Madinah in Rabi‘ al-Awwal 11 AH and was buried in his house beside the mosque.
events.significance: The completion of revelation and the end of prophethood.

events.title: Caliphate of Abu Bakr (RA)
events.summary: The first caliph reunited Arabia during the Ridda wars and ordered the first compilation of the Quran.
events.description: Chosen at Saqifah Banu Sa‘idah, Abu Bakr confronted tribes who withheld zakat or followed false prophets. After many huffaz died at Yamamah, Zayd ibn Thabit compiled the Quran into a single codex.
events.significance: Secured the survival of the Muslim community after the Prophet ﷺ.

events.title: Caliphate of Umar ibn al-Khattab (RA)
events.summary: Umar expanded the state into Syria, Iraq, Persia and Egypt and built its institutions.
events.description: He established the diwan (registers), the Hijri calendar, garrison cities like Kufa and Basra, and received the keys of Jerusalem in 637/638, guaranteeing the safety of its Christians.
events.significance: Turned the caliphate into an organised empire known for justice.

events.title: Battle of Yarmouk
events.summary: Khalid ibn al-Walid’s forces decisively defeated the Byzantine army.
events.description: The six-day battle ended Byzantine rule in Syria and opened the Levant to Muslim rule.
events.significance: One of the most decisive battles in world history.

events.title: Battle of al-Qadisiyyah
events.summary: Sa‘d ibn Abi Waqqas defeated the Sasanian Persian army.
events.description: The victory opened Iraq and led to the fall of Ctesiphon and, by 651, the end of the Sasanian Empire.
events.significance: Brought Persia into the Islamic world.

events.title: Caliphate of Uthman (RA) and the Standard Mushaf
events.summary: Uthman standardised the written Quran and sent copies to the major cities.
events.description: He expanded the navy and the frontiers into North Africa and Armenia. Political discontent ended with his assassination in Madinah in 656.
events.significance: The Uthmanic codex is the basis of every Quran today.

events.title: Caliphate of Ali (RA)
events.summary: Ali moved the capital to Kufa amid the first civil war (fitnah).
events.description: His caliphate saw the Battles of the Camel and Siffin and arbitration with Mu‘awiya. He was assassinated in Kufa in 661, ending the Rashidun era.
events.significance: The end of the Rightly Guided Caliphs and the origin of later sectarian divisions.

events.title: Umayyad Caliphate Founded in Damascus
events.summary: Mu‘awiya founded a hereditary dynasty with its capital at Damascus.
events.description: The Umayyads built the largest empire the world had yet seen, from Iberia to Sindh. Arabic became the language of administration and coinage was reformed under Abd al-Malik.
events.significance: Transformed the caliphate into a world empire.

events.title: Tragedy of Karbala
events.summary: Husayn ibn Ali, grandson of the Prophet ﷺ, was martyred with his family and companions.
events.description: Refusing to pledge allegiance to Yazid, Husayn set out for Kufa and was surrounded at Karbala. His martyrdom on Ashura is mourned across the Muslim world.
events.significance: A defining event for Muslim conscience and especially for Shi‘a Islam.

events.title: Dome of the Rock Completed
events.summary: Abd al-Malik built the earliest surviving great work of Islamic architecture.
events.description: The octagonal shrine over the Foundation Stone features mosaics and Quranic inscriptions. It stands on the Haram al-Sharif beside al-Aqsa Mosque.
events.significance: An enduring symbol of Jerusalem and early Islamic art.

events.title: Tariq ibn Ziyad Crosses to Iberia
events.summary: Muslim forces crossed from North Africa and conquered most of the Iberian Peninsula.
events.description: Tariq ibn Ziyad defeated King Roderic at Guadalete. Al-Andalus became a centre of Islamic civilisation for nearly 800 years.
events.significance: Gave Gibraltar its name (Jabal Tariq) and began al-Andalus.

events.title: Muhammad bin Qasim in Sindh
events.summary: An Umayyad army conquered Sindh and Multan, bringing Islam into South Asia as a ruling power.
events.description: Sent by Hajjaj ibn Yusuf, the young commander defeated Raja Dahir. Sindh remained under caliphal governors for centuries.
events.significance: The first Muslim political presence in the Indian subcontinent.

events.title: Abbasid Revolution and Founding of Baghdad
events.summary: The Abbasids overthrew the Umayyads; al-Mansur founded Baghdad as the "City of Peace".
events.description: The new capital became the largest city in the world and the hub of trade between China, India, Africa and Europe. Persian administrative traditions blended with Arab culture.
events.significance: Inaugurated the classical age of Islamic civilisation.

events.title: Great Mosque of Córdoba and Umayyad al-Andalus
events.summary: Abd al-Rahman I, a surviving Umayyad prince, founded an emirate in Córdoba and its great mosque.
events.description: Córdoba became the largest and most cultured city of Western Europe, with libraries, paved streets and street lighting. Abd al-Rahman III declared a caliphate in 929.
events.significance: A bridge transferring knowledge into medieval Europe.

events.title: Fatimids Found Cairo and al-Azhar
events.summary: The Fatimid caliphate built Cairo (al-Qahirah) and the al-Azhar mosque in 970.
events.description: Al-Azhar developed into one of the oldest continuously operating universities and a leading centre of Sunni scholarship after the Ayyubid period.
events.significance: Made Cairo a political and intellectual capital of the Muslim world.

events.title: Seljuks and the Battle of Manzikert
events.summary: Seljuk Sultan Alp Arslan defeated and captured Byzantine Emperor Romanos IV.
events.description: The victory opened Anatolia to Turkish settlement and prompted Byzantine appeals that led to the Crusades.
events.significance: The beginning of Turkish Anatolia.

events.title: Salahuddin, Hattin and Jerusalem
events.summary: Salahuddin al-Ayyubi defeated the Crusaders and recovered Jerusalem.
events.description: After 88 years of Crusader rule (from 1099), Salahuddin retook Jerusalem with notable restraint, allowing ransomed inhabitants to leave. The Third Crusade under Richard I followed.
events.significance: A celebrated model of chivalry in both Muslim and European memory.

events.title: Mongol Sack of Baghdad
events.summary: Hulagu Khan’s Mongols destroyed Baghdad and killed the Abbasid caliph.
events.description: Libraries including the House of Wisdom were destroyed and a large part of the population was massacred. The Abbasid line continued as figurehead caliphs under the Mamluks in Cairo.
events.significance: Often seen as the symbolic end of the Islamic Golden Age.

events.title: Battle of Ain Jalut
events.summary: The Mamluks under Qutuz and Baybars defeated the Mongols.
events.description: The first major Mongol defeat in open battle stopped their advance into Egypt and preserved the Mamluk Sultanate as the centre of the Arab world.
events.significance: Saved Egypt and North Africa from Mongol conquest.

events.title: Bayt al-Hikma – House of Wisdom
events.summary: Abbasid Baghdad became the centre of translation, science and philosophy.
events.description: Under Harun al-Rashid and al-Ma’mun, scholars like Hunayn ibn Ishaq translated Greek, Persian and Indian works into Arabic. Paper-making, learned from China via Samarkand, made books abundant.
events.significance: Preserved and extended classical knowledge for the world.

events.title: Al-Khwarizmi and the Birth of Algebra
events.summary: His book al-Jabr gave algebra its name; his own name gives us "algorithm".
events.description: Al-Khwarizmi systematised solving linear and quadratic equations and popularised Hindu-Arabic numerals with zero, which reached Europe via Latin translations.
events.significance: Foundations of algebra and computer science.

events.title: Fatima al-Fihri Founds al-Qarawiyyin
events.summary: A woman founded what UNESCO and Guinness call the oldest existing, continually operating university.
events.description: Fatima al-Fihri used her inheritance to build a mosque that grew into a great centre of learning in theology, law, astronomy and medicine.
events.significance: A landmark in the history of education and women’s patronage.

events.title: Al-Razi – Physician of Rayy
events.summary: Al-Razi first distinguished smallpox from measles and ran hospitals in Rayy and Baghdad.
events.description: His encyclopedic al-Hawi and clinical observations made him one of the greatest physicians of the medieval world.
events.significance: Pioneer of clinical medicine.

events.title: Ibn al-Haytham’s Book of Optics
events.summary: Ibn al-Haytham showed that vision results from light entering the eye and stressed experiment.
events.description: His Kitab al-Manazir studied reflection, refraction and the camera obscura. He is often called a pioneer of the scientific method.
events.significance: Transformed the science of optics.

events.title: Ibn Sina’s Canon of Medicine
events.summary: The Canon of Medicine was a standard medical textbook in Europe and the Islamic world for centuries.
events.description: Ibn Sina (Avicenna) was also a major philosopher whose work on logic and metaphysics deeply influenced both Islamic and Latin thought.
events.significance: One of the most influential scholars in history.

events.title: Al-Biruni Studies India
events.summary: Al-Biruni wrote a remarkably objective study of Indian religion, science and society.
events.description: He calculated Earth’s radius with high accuracy using a mountain-top method and wrote on astronomy, geography and comparative religion.
events.significance: Founding figure of comparative religion and Indology.

events.title: Al-Ghazali’s Revival of the Religious Sciences
events.summary: Al-Ghazali reconciled law, theology and Sufism in the Ihya’ ‘Ulum al-Din.
events.description: After teaching at the Nizamiyya of Baghdad he left on a spiritual journey, writing works that shaped Sunni thought for centuries.
events.significance: One of the most influential Muslim thinkers.

events.title: Ibn Rushd (Averroes)
events.summary: The great commentator on Aristotle, jurist and physician of al-Andalus.
events.description: Ibn Rushd defended philosophy in "The Incoherence of the Incoherence". His commentaries strongly influenced Latin scholasticism.
events.significance: A key link between Islamic and European philosophy.

events.title: Islamic Trade Networks of the Indian Ocean
events.summary: Muslim merchants linked East Africa, Arabia, India, Southeast Asia and China.
events.description: Dhows sailed with the monsoon winds carrying spices, textiles, ceramics and ideas. Islam spread peacefully through traders to the Swahili coast, Bengal, Malacca and the Indonesian islands.
events.significance: Made Islam the faith of the world’s largest maritime trading network.

events.title: Mansa Musa’s Pilgrimage
events.summary: The ruler of Mali travelled to Makkah with so much gold that it affected prices in Cairo.
events.description: Mansa Musa built the Djinguereber mosque in Timbuktu and brought scholars back to Mali, making Timbuktu a centre of Islamic learning.
events.significance: Put West Africa on the map of the medieval world.

events.title: Travels of Ibn Battuta
events.summary: The Moroccan scholar travelled about 120,000 km across the Muslim world and beyond.
events.description: Over 29 years he visited West Africa, the Middle East, Central Asia, India, Bengal, the Maldives and China. His Rihla is a unique record of the 14th-century world.
events.significance: The greatest traveller of the pre-modern era.

events.title: Ibn Khaldun’s Muqaddimah
events.summary: A pioneering work of historiography, sociology and economics.
events.description: Ibn Khaldun analysed the rise and fall of dynasties through ‘asabiyyah (group solidarity) and examined economics, labour and urbanisation.
events.significance: Often regarded as a founder of social science.

events.title: Founding of the Ottoman State
events.summary: Osman I founded a small principality in north-western Anatolia that became a world empire.
events.description: The Ottomans expanded into the Balkans and Anatolia, surviving defeat by Timur in 1402 to become the leading Muslim power for six centuries.
events.significance: The longest-lasting Islamic empire.

events.title: Conquest of Constantinople
events.summary: Sultan Mehmed II captured the Byzantine capital, which became Istanbul.
events.description: Massive cannons breached the Theodosian Walls after a 53-day siege. Hagia Sophia was converted into a mosque and Istanbul became the Ottoman capital.
events.significance: Ended the Byzantine Empire; often used to mark the end of the Middle Ages.

events.title: Fall of Granada
events.summary: The last Muslim kingdom of Iberia surrendered to Ferdinand and Isabella.
events.description: Muhammad XII (Boabdil) handed over the Alhambra. Despite the treaty, Muslims and Jews faced forced conversion and expulsion in the following decades.
events.significance: The end of nearly 800 years of al-Andalus.

events.title: Safavid Empire Founded
events.summary: Shah Ismail I founded the Safavid state and made Twelver Shi‘ism the state religion of Iran.
events.description: The Safavids fought the Ottomans at Chaldiran (1514) and shaped modern Iranian identity.
events.significance: Created the basis of modern Iran.

events.title: Shah Abbas and Isfahan "Half the World"
events.summary: Shah Abbas the Great moved the capital to Isfahan and built the Naqsh-e Jahan Square.
events.description: The square, with the Shah Mosque and Sheikh Lotfollah Mosque, was the heart of a city famous for its silk trade and craftsmanship. "Isfahan nesf-e jahan" (Isfahan is half the world).
events.significance: A UNESCO World Heritage Site and peak of Persian Islamic art.

events.title: Suleiman the Magnificent
events.summary: Known as Kanuni (the Lawgiver), Suleiman brought the Ottomans to their height.
events.description: He conquered Belgrade, Rhodes, Baghdad and Hungary, besieged Vienna in 1529, and codified law. The architect Mimar Sinan built the Süleymaniye Mosque.
events.significance: The golden age of Ottoman power and culture.

events.title: First Battle of Panipat – Mughal Empire Founded
events.summary: Babur defeated Ibrahim Lodi, founding the Mughal Empire.
events.description: Babur, a descendant of Timur and Genghis Khan, used field artillery and the tulughma flanking tactic. The Mughals ruled much of South Asia for over two centuries.
events.significance: The beginning of the Mughal Empire.

events.title: Akbar the Great
events.summary: Akbar expanded the empire and created an efficient administrative and revenue system.
events.description: His mansabdari system and Raja Todar Mal’s land revenue reforms shaped Mughal governance. He promoted religious dialogue and conquered Bengal in 1576. The Bengali calendar (Bangabda) was reorganised under his reign.
events.significance: Consolidated the Mughal Empire.

events.title: Taj Mahal Built
events.summary: Shah Jahan built a white marble mausoleum for his wife Mumtaz Mahal.
events.description: Designed by Ustad Ahmad Lahauri and built by some 20,000 artisans, the Taj Mahal is considered the jewel of Muslim art in India.
events.significance: A UNESCO World Heritage Site and global icon.

events.title: Reign of Aurangzeb
events.summary: The Mughal Empire reached its greatest extent under Aurangzeb.
events.description: He compiled the Fatawa-e-Alamgiri and fought long wars in the Deccan. After his death in 1707 the empire fragmented into regional states such as Bengal, Hyderabad and Awadh.
events.significance: Peak and turning point of Mughal power.

events.title: Siege of Vienna
events.summary: The Ottoman siege of Vienna was broken by a relief army under Jan III Sobieski.
events.description: The defeat began a long Ottoman retreat from central Europe, confirmed by the Treaty of Karlowitz (1699).
events.significance: The high-water mark of Ottoman expansion in Europe.

events.title: European Colonialism in the Muslim World
events.summary: From Napoleon’s invasion of Egypt to the end of the Mughals, most Muslim lands came under European rule.
events.description: France took Algeria (1830), Britain ended the Mughal dynasty (1857), and the Dutch ruled the East Indies. Reform movements such as Deoband (1866), Aligarh (1875) and the Salafiyya of al-Afghani and Muhammad Abduh responded in different ways.
events.significance: Shaped the borders, politics and intellectual life of the modern Muslim world.

events.title: End of the Ottoman Empire and Abolition of the Caliphate
events.summary: The Turkish Grand National Assembly abolished the sultanate (1922) and the caliphate (1924).
events.description: After defeat in World War I and the Turkish War of Independence, Mustafa Kemal Atatürk founded the Republic of Turkey. The Khilafat movement in British India had campaigned to save the caliphate.
events.significance: Ended the institution of the caliphate after some 1,300 years.

references.title: Wikipedia – Abolition of the Ottoman Caliphate

events.title: Kingdom of Saudi Arabia Established
events.summary: Abdulaziz ibn Saud unified the Hejaz and Najd into Saudi Arabia.
events.description: Oil was discovered in 1938, transforming the economy and the infrastructure serving the Two Holy Mosques and Hajj pilgrims.
events.significance: Custodianship of Makkah and Madinah under the modern Saudi state.

events.title: Pakistan: First State Founded in the Name of Islam
events.summary: Pakistan was created as a homeland for Muslims of the subcontinent, including East Bengal.
events.description: Inspired by thinkers like Muhammad Iqbal and led by Muhammad Ali Jinnah, Pakistan at its founding was the largest Muslim-majority state in the world. Its eastern wing later became Bangladesh in 1971.
events.significance: A major milestone of Muslim political independence.

events.title: Organisation of Islamic Cooperation Founded
events.summary: Muslim states formed the OIC after an arson attack on al-Aqsa Mosque.
events.description: Founded in Rabat, the OIC now has 57 member states, making it the second-largest intergovernmental organisation after the UN. Bangladesh joined in 1974.
events.significance: The collective voice of the Muslim world.

events.title: Beginning of the 15th Hijri Century (1400 AH)
events.summary: The new Hijri century opened in a year of upheaval: the Iranian Revolution and the Grand Mosque seizure.
events.description: In February 1979 the Iranian Revolution established an Islamic Republic. On 1 Muharram 1400 militants seized the Masjid al-Haram in Makkah; the siege ended after two weeks. The Soviet invasion of Afghanistan followed in December.
events.significance: A turning point for political Islam in the modern era.

events.title: Rise of Islamic Finance
events.summary: Interest-free banking grew from a few experiments into a global industry.
events.description: The Islamic Development Bank (1975) and Dubai Islamic Bank (1975) were followed by many others, including Islami Bank Bangladesh (1983). Sukuk bonds and takaful insurance spread worldwide.
events.significance: An economic expression of Islamic ethics in modern markets.

events.title: The Contemporary Muslim World
events.summary: About 1.9–2 billion Muslims live today, the majority in Asia.
events.description: Indonesia, Pakistan, India and Bangladesh have the largest Muslim populations. The period has seen the Arab Spring (2010–2012), conflicts in Syria, Iraq, Yemen and Gaza, mass migration, and rapid growth in Islamic education and digital religious media.
events.significance: Islam is the world’s second-largest and fastest-growing religion.

events.title: Invention of Writing in Sumer
events.summary: Cuneiform script developed in Uruk for record-keeping.
events.description: Scribes pressed wedge-shaped marks into clay tablets, first for accounts, later for law, literature (the Epic of Gilgamesh) and science.
events.significance: The beginning of recorded history.

events.title: Unification of Egypt
events.summary: King Narmer (Menes) united Upper and Lower Egypt.
events.description: The Narmer Palette shows the king wearing both crowns. Memphis became the capital of a state that lasted nearly 3,000 years.
events.significance: One of the world’s first nation-states.

events.title: Indus Valley Civilisation
events.summary: Planned cities with grid streets, drains and standardised bricks flourished on the Indus.
events.description: Mohenjo-daro and Harappa had the Great Bath, granaries and an undeciphered script. The civilisation traded with Mesopotamia.
events.significance: South Asia’s first urban civilisation.

events.title: Great Pyramid of Giza
events.summary: Built for Pharaoh Khufu, it was the tallest human-made structure for over 3,800 years.
